briefFidelity: FAIL, and the disagreement is total rather than partial. The brief opens 'No subject at all... nothing should invite a viewer to name it.' Before I had read a word of it I named this work three separate ways in my own description: an X-ray or scan with a metal fragment showing through soft tissue, a stone with an amber inclusion, and a wrapped bundle with splints strapped across it. It did not resist naming, it volunteered it, and it does so most strongly in exactly the seeds that are otherwise best made (9011, 9369, 9548, 10801, 10264), where a tall two-lobed grey body sits centred on black with a hot amber object lodged in the middle of it. The brief then asks for an all-over field with even distribution and no single dominant element, figure explicitly ruled out in favour of ground; what is here is a figure on a ground in eleven of twelve seeds, with black margin all round and a clear three-step hierarchy of amber core, then grey body, then scatter. It asks for a narrow tonal palette of close values so that differences read as spacing rather than colour; the actual range runs from near-black ground through bone-white slabs (9727, 10622) and hangs the entire read on one saturated amber hue, so the differences read as colour and as nothing else. It asks the market to act on the DENSITY of the field, more or fewer marks, visibly at browse size; what the market actually does is lighten and desaturate a wash while the mark count, positions and silhouette stay fixed. Four clauses, four misses. Only the last sentence of the brief, that tokens differ in the count and placement of their marks, is partly honoured, and only by the scatter squares.
composition: Judged against this brief it fails, and it fails by being good at the opposite thing. Every tile is centred, vertical, roughly bilaterally balanced and floating with black margin on all four sides; 9011, 9369, 9548, 10264 and 10801 are portraits of an object, not fields. The dominant element is unmissable and deliberate: the amber core is the only hue and the only hard edge in the frame, so the eye lands on it first in every seed. The brief asked for balance without symmetry and no dominant element; this delivers near-symmetry with a strong dominant. 9906 and 10085 come closest to an even distribution of incident, and 10622 is the only tile that engages the frame edge at all, but 10622 reads as cropped rather than as composed. The frame is otherwise unused: the work sits in the middle of it.
collectionCoherence: The strongest axis, and a genuine pass on its own terms. All twelve share one ground, one three-part vocabulary (translucent grey capsule mass, amber angular core or planks, hard-edged square and diamond scatter), one colour law and one vertical portrait posture. Even the outliers stay inside the grammar: 9906 keeps the amber and the scatter while dissolving the body to a ghost, and 10085 keeps the knot and the ring of squares while shrinking the mass almost away. Laid out together 9011, 9369, 9548, 9727, 10264 and 10801 are plainly siblings, and 9190, 10443 and 10980 are the same family with the core exploded into struts. Nobody would mistake this contact sheet for a folder.
palette: Chosen, controlled and handsome, and wrong for what was asked. It is a two-register scheme: a full greyscale run from near-black ground through slate, ash and bone-white (the white slabs in 9727 and 10622 are the brightest thing on either sheet), plus one amber-ochre hue used only on the core and the planks. That is a wide value range, not close values, and the single hue is doing the entire job of drawing the eye, which is precisely the 'differences read as colour' the brief rules out. The ground supports rather than competes, and the translucency law that lightens the mass where capsules overlap is a real and pleasing invention at 256 in 9011 and 10801. But narrow and tonal it is not.
seedVariation: Real, and comfortably inside the healthy band between twelve rotations and twelve unrelated works. The range runs from 9369 and 10801, which are quiet grey bodies with a small compact core and no scatter, through 9548 and 10264 where the core swells to a third of the body, to 10443's thin radiating spokes, 9190 and 10980's diagonal planks, 9727's columns of tiles down both margins, 10085's floating knot in a ring of squares, and out to 9906 and 10622 at the loud end. What it is NOT is variation in the count and placement of marks in a field, which is the variation the brief specified; it is variation in the amplitude and form of one recurring figure. The scatter squares do vary in count and placement seed to seed, so the clause is touched, but it is touched by the least important element in the frame.
thumbnailSurvival: The seed sheet survives 120px better than most work of this density: the amber carries, and the twelve are still separable as twelve — the quiet pair (9369, 10801), the loud cores (9548, 10264), the spokes (10443), the plank seeds (9190, 10980, 9906), the ringed knot (10085), the bordered one (9727) and the cluttered one (10622) all hold their identity. What is lost is the layering: the overlapping translucent capsules that give 9011 and 10801 their depth at 256 merge into one flat grey slab at 120, so the body becomes a plain blob and the vellum quality is gone. The state sheet does not survive at all, which is the failure that matters here.
marketResponse: FAIL, on both halves of the requirement. The brief names density as the channel: more marks under drawdown, fewer in recovery or the reverse, visibly at browse size. Across 9011, 9190, 9369 and 9548 no mark is ever added or removed and nothing changes position; the count, the layout, the silhouette and the orientation are identical in all three rows. What actually changes is a tonal wash — under stress the dark underlayers of the grey mass lift toward mid-grey so the body flattens and hazes and the amber desaturates a little; under recovery the mass stays light while the amber returns stronger and slightly broader than neutral, clearest in 9548 and 9369. That is a legible transition at 256 if you look for it. At 120 it is not there: 9011 neutral, stress and recovery are the same picture, 9190 and 9369 likewise, and only 9548 differs at all, by its core being marginally wider. Shuffle the three rows of the 120 sheet and I could not sort them back. The brief also asked for the change the work does not make and did not ask for the one it makes.
tokenIdentity: Passes easily, and for the wrong reason. 9011 is unmistakably 9011 in all three states, 9190 keeps its exact jackstraw arrangement of planks, 9369 keeps its small centred core and its two pale shoulder slabs, and 9548 keeps its broad spiky knot. Nothing is replaced by another object under drawdown. But the identity is preserved because so little happens: with mark count, position and silhouette all frozen, identity was never at risk. This axis and marketResponse are measuring the same absence from opposite sides, and a work that is this safe on one is usually this thin on the other.
artifacts: Few and minor. 10622's white and grey slabs are cut hard by the top and bottom tile edges and read as clipping rather than as a decision — it is the one tile that looks like a viewBox accident. The pale slabs that sit exactly on the left and right shoulders of the mass in 9011, 9369 and 9727 read as a seam or a UI chrome element rather than as part of the body, especially at 120 where 9369's look like tabs stuck to the sides. The amber planks in 9190, 9906 and 10980 overshoot the grey mass and terminate in mid-air at no meaningful point. Nothing collapses into mush, no stroke vanishes, edges are clean throughout, and the overlap maths of the translucent capsules is consistent everywhere I looked.
reasoning: This is competent, coherent, attractive work and it is not the work that was commissioned. The brief is INTERVAL: no subject, nothing nameable, an all-over field with no dominant element, close tonal values so that differences read as spacing, and a market that acts on the density of the field visibly at browse size. Written before I had read any of that, my own description named the thing three times over — an X-ray, a stone with an inclusion, a bundle with splints — described a centred figure floating on a ground with a clear focal hierarchy, described a palette running from near-black to bone-white hung on a single saturated amber accent, and recorded that across all three states nothing enters, nothing leaves and nothing moves. That is four of the brief's clauses contradicted by an unanchored reading of the pictures, and briefFidelity is a gate. The single sentence that decided it: the brief asks for a field whose only content is the relationship between marks, and what is on these sheets is an object with a hot centre that every viewer will name within a second of seeing it. The density failure compounds it rather than causing it — the market response is a saturation wash, not a change in mark count, and at 120px, the size the brief explicitly names, it is not visible at all.
wouldChange: Three concrete changes, in order of importance. First, kill the figure: the vertical two-lobed capsule mass is the subject and it has to go, replaced by marks distributed across the whole tile including the corners and edges, so that 9369 and 10801 stop being portraits with black margin and become fields. The scatter squares already in 9727, 10085 and 10980 are the right raw element; they should be the whole work rather than a border around the real one. Second, compress the palette to what was asked: drop the saturated amber entirely or desaturate it into the greyscale run, and pull the bone-whites of 9727 and 10622 down toward the ground so that no mark is the obvious focus and the eye reads spacing instead of hue. Third, move the market onto count: bind the state to the NUMBER of marks rather than to fill opacity and saturation, with a spread big enough that a 120px stress tile is visibly denser or sparser than its neutral — the current wash in 9011 and 9190 is invisible at browse size and would have to change by a large multiple of marks, not a few percent of alpha, to register. Keep the translucent-overlap lightening law and the scatter geometry; they are the two genuinely good inventions here and both would survive the transplant.
